text: France, on the eve of a revolution, and two young women need a doctor. The plague that killed their parents left Louise blind, so she and Henriette, raised together as sisters, set out for Paris and a cure; a lustful aristocrat separates them almost as soon as they arrive. What follows spends its hundred and fifty minutes on that separation rather than on the barricades. The Revolution is weather here: it gathers in streets people are already crossing for reasons of their own, and it turns an ordinary search for one missing person into something that can get a person killed. Griffith is unembarrassed by melodrama, the fainting and the coincidence and the hand that misses by inches. Underneath sits a hard arithmetic. Two women in one city, and nothing but luck to bring them together.

A film director needs one little girl, and the corridor at Cinecittà is full of mothers holding their daughters by the wrist. Maddelena is one of them, and the film is an account of what she will spend to get Maria through the next door: money she does not have, lessons, favors, the afternoons of a child nobody thought to ask. Visconti keeps the register near farce, and it is not a kind farce - the queue, the screen test, the men who decide are all filmed as a working system rather than a dream. Italy's own preservationists count it among a hundred films the country should not lose. What complicates everything is how sympathetic Maddelena stays. She is not deceived about the business; she has watched it long enough to know what a face is worth there, and that is what makes her push.

A woman wanted by the police takes a job standing knee-deep in water. Francesca and her partner Walter are small-time criminals, and her way of disappearing is to sign on with a crew of women rice workers in the north of Italy, where the labor is done bent over a flooded field, in ranks. Giuseppe De Santis films that work with documentary patience, then films Silvana, the young worker Francesca falls in beside, in an entirely different key, closer to a magazine cover. The friction between those two ways of looking is the real subject. Walter does not stay away long, a soldier finishing his service turns up as well, and four people with four incompatible plans end up circling a single harvest. It won an Academy Award for its story. The story is the least interesting thing in it.

Everything here proceeds from a piece of reasoning, and the reasoning is the frightening part. A young man with epilepsy, inside a family that has stopped functioning, concludes that the household would be better off with fewer people in it, and he reaches that conclusion the way a person reaches a chore: as a service someone ought to perform, kindly. The premise would support horror. Marco Bellocchio keeps it at the level of domestic routine instead, which puts the pressure on small things - who is at the table, who is being managed, how much of a day in that house goes to waiting for nothing in particular. Nobody in it is a monster and nobody is looking after anyone. A hundred and ten minutes is a long time in one family's rooms, and the film is fully aware of the length.

Louis gets out of prison and does well - legitimate work first, then better work, then a phonograph factory of his own, which he sets about mechanizing at once. René Clair's 1931 comedy took its Academy Award for production design, and design is where the argument actually sits, because the joke only lands if a shop floor can be made to feel like the yard Louis walked a few reels earlier. Then Émile finishes his own sentence and turns up, cheerful and inconvenient, and the question becomes how much of a life a man is allowed to leave behind. Much of the picture is movement rather than talk: pursuit, ranks, timing, songs doing the work dialogue would do elsewhere. It never once sneers at Louis for having wanted the money.

Being the least impressive member of the most important family in town is a specific kind of trouble. The youngest son cannot out-work his father or out-fight his brothers, so the 1927 comedy built around him leaves him one resource: invention, the narrow margin available to anyone everybody has already sized up. A woman new to town does not yet know where he ranks, and her ignorance is worth more to him than the family name ever was. Eighty-two silent minutes have no space for a speech about self-respect, so the gags carry it - the physical logic of a boy improvising an authority nobody handed him, in a place where reputation is inherited along with the land. Ted Wilde directed. At issue is one man's opinion of his son, treated as the only currency in circulation.

An American missionary is held in Shanghai by a warlord who treats her as a guest, and the film is not much interested in her rescue. Frank Capra directed it in 1933: eighty-seven minutes, mostly indoors, a seduction conducted through courtesy - meals, argument, the manners of a captivity that never says its name. What she believes about herself, that she came to be useful and is otherwise untouched, is what the picture keeps pressing on from the side, patiently, without raising its voice. The result is a strange object, a romance whose pleasures are atmospheric and whose discomfort is inhabited rather than resolved. She is the one being altered, and the last to know it, which is not a flattering thing for a studio picture to say about its heroine.

The troupe is not good, and everyone in it knows, beginning with the man who runs it. Checco Dal Monte keeps a variety company moving between small-town dates on heart and habit, and the arrangement holds because nobody in it has a better offer. Then Lily joins as a dancer and the houses start selling out. Alberto Lattuada's 1950 film is about what one person's real prospect does to a group that has none: Checco's mistress watching the billing change, the daily humiliation of being carried, how fast loyalty gets re-priced. Lily is not a villain. She is simply looking further up the road than anyone else in the company. Ninety-three minutes, backstage and between towns, and the ache comes from how modest all these ambitions were to start with.

A jacket, handed to a stranger out of kindness, with a winning lottery ticket still in the pocket. Michel is a painter who owes money across Paris and has just come into a million florins he cannot reach; Béatrice meant well; an elderly thief now owns the coat; and Prosper, Michel's rival, works out the situation at roughly the moment everyone else does. René Clair turns the pursuit into music. The chase is sung and scored, sound in 1931 used as rhythm rather than conversation, and the eighty-three minutes are assembled like a mechanism, everybody arriving in the wrong room at the right time. Comedy this precise is easy to undervalue, because nothing in it looks difficult. The coat keeps moving, and the city goes on with its business around it.

A rich husband pays to have his wife's past looked into, and the inquiry produces exactly what it was meant to rule out. It puts her back in a room with the man she loved before him. Michelangelo Antonioni made this in 1950, and the tempo is already strange for a picture with a crime in it: waiting, walking, conversations held in the wrong places because two people who are recognized cannot be alone anywhere. The money is not incidental. She has a house, an account, clothes, an arrangement that any decision at all would cost her outright, and the film keeps that arithmetic in front of her during every hour she is not being watched. It borrows the shape of a thriller and withholds the relief a thriller supplies. Nobody raises a voice. The wealth does not need to.

A young woman leaves the countryside for Rome to be looked at for a living. What follows is neither a warning nor a fall; Antonio Pietrangeli seems most interested in the texture of her days, the relentless pleasantness of people who want something from her, and the good humour she keeps intact throughout. That good humour is the hard part, and it is also what the men around her take as permission. She is not stupid and she is not innocent. She has decided this is the price of the thing she wants, and she pays it in small installments, wherever the business conducts its actual business. A hundred and fifteen minutes, made in 1965, and the unkindness is cumulative: no single scene would look like damage if it were shown on its own.

Forty-three minutes, one marriage, and a plan the wife keeps entirely to herself. She cannot stand her husband, she works out a way to be rid of him, and the film hands her that thought early, then stays with her while she carries it around the house like an errand not yet run. The brevity does real work: at this length there is no room for the backstory that would explain her, so the marriage has to be legible in gesture alone - how a person sits, what her hands do while somebody else is talking, the exact quality of a smile produced on request. Germaine Dulac directed it in 1923, and the attention is entirely inward; the husband registers less as a character than as a set of habits she has memorized. The scheme matters less than the patience.

A man comes home, decides to cook for himself, and takes his time about it. Hidden somewhere in that kitchen is a revolver which may once have belonged to John Dillinger, the only event in the film, and it alters the pace of the evening not at all. Marco Ferreri gives ninety-five minutes to a single domestic interior and the small industry of an ordinary night inside it: what gets prepared, what gets handled, what is done simply because the hours are there to be filled. The gun refuses to organize the story the way guns organize stories. It becomes one more object in a house already full of objects, and the disquiet comes from how comfortable the man is having it near him. The claim about Dillinger may be worth nothing. The revolver is not nothing.

The parents did vaudeville, and the children have the trade in them with no stage to use it on. So Mickey Moran sets about building one, with his girlfriend Patsy in the act and Rosalie, a former child star after a comeback, wanting the part and the boy both. Busby Berkeley directed this in 1939, and the plot is thin on purpose; it is friction enough to hang ninety-three minutes of numbers on. What survives the sentiment is the work. These are performers raised to rehearse, and the film keeps coming back to the making of the thing, the arranging and borrowing and persuading, a show treated as something built rather than wished for. The feeling runs thick and unashamed. The energy under it belongs to kids who know the family business does not pass down on its own.
